source.title: Predicting the outputs of finite deep neural networks trained with noisy gradients.
source.authors: Gadi Naveh; Oded Ben-David; H. Sompolinsky; Z. Ringel

record.file_problem: None noted; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares finite-width CNN test performance with the corresponding NNGP, using a distinct training protocol. It does not test the specific behaviors named in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper reports finite-CNN versus NNGP test-loss results on CIFAR-10. Its comparisons with fully connected networks and standard SGD are cited prior work, not its own results. Figure-based results are described qualitatively in the text; precise plotted values are unavailable here.
record.test_reason: The study tests finite-network versus NNGP predictions and test MSE under Langevin training, but none of V1–V8. Its width experiments do not establish zero training error and use explicit weight decay; they therefore do not test V2. CNN-versus-FCN performance comparisons are cited work, not its own results.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly correct. More precisely, the authors establish a Langevin-trained network–stochastic-process correspondence and derive finite-width corrections that improve prediction of network outputs over the NNGP approximation. They also demonstrate a finite-CNN test-MSE advantage over NNGPs on CIFAR-10. Better approximation of network outputs does not itself imply improved test performance in every setting.
record.recipe_differences: Full-batch gradient descent with externally injected Gaussian noise and weight decay, rather than standard gradient training; evaluates finite-width CNNs against corresponding NNGPs.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the finite-CNN/NNGP performance gap changes with channel count. It also notes that learning-rate discretization can destabilize some settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Finite CNNs have lower CIFAR-10 test MSE than their corresponding NNGPs in tested settings; performance deteriorates at large channel counts toward the NNGP limit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the tested Langevin training and output-averaging protocol, finite-width CNNs without pooling can outperform their corresponding NNGPs, with the advantage diminishing at large width.

record.problems: The CIFAR-10 experiments use the paper’s specialized noisy-gradient protocol, not standard SGD. The plotted results are provided without recoverable per-width numeric values in the supplied text; the authors also report statistical error tied to output averaging, not random test-set choice, for Fig. 7.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level held-out performance compared with natural-label generalization.
Held-out classification error beyond the width required for zero training error without explicit regularization.
Comparative image-classification performance of convolutional and fully connected networks, including the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a predictor of generalization gaps.
Test-accuracy effects of removing memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: The large-width deterioration is not a challenge to V2 because its defining interpolation and training conditions are not established here. Appendix I distinguishes CNNs from locally connected networks through fourth cumulants, but supplies no CNN-versus-FCN test-error comparison for V3.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization under standard training.
Test error as width increases beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Finite convolutional versus fully connected networks, local connectivity, and learned sparse connections.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and their held-out performance.
Large versus small batch training and the effect of adapting the recipe.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other measures as predictors of the train–test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.note: The text describes the result qualitatively; exact plotted values are not provided.
rows.check: The finite-CNN advantage over its NNGP is reported, but measures no supplied version. The outcome is MSE of averaged outputs, not classification error. Appendix G specifies 2000 test points.

rows.operation_detail: Compared finite-width CNN test loss with that of its corresponding NNGP across channel counts.
rows.measure: MSE test loss; discrepancy between CNN and GP outputs
rows.value: performance deteriorates at large N = #Channels as the NNSP associated with the CNN approaches an NNGP
rows.uncertainty: Error bars reflect statistical errors related only to output averaging and not due to the random choice of a test-set.
rows.note: The caption reports the qualitative trend and a discrepancy slope of −1.77 for the largest channel count reached, but does not give the plotted per-width test-loss values.
rows.check: The reported large-width deterioration is valid for this CNN–NNGP comparison, but does not establish incomplete expression of any supplied version. Zero training error is not demonstrated, explicit weight decay is used, and the measure is test MSE.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
